## Question 1

### Part a
#### 1

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(354)

R <- 1000
simulations <- vector("list", R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  simulations[[i]] <- data.frame(
    value = rnorm(150, mean = 0, sd = 1),
    group = factor(rep(1:5, each = 30))
  )
}
```
:::


#### 2

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
error_unadjusted <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  test_unadjusted <- pairwise.t.test(
    dat$value, dat$group,
    p.adjust.method = "none"
  )

  error_unadjusted[i] <- any(
    test_unadjusted$p.value < 0.05,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}

mean(error_unadjusted)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.294
```


:::
:::


At least one pairwise comparison provided statistically discernible
support for a non-zero mean difference in
294 of the 1,000 simulations (p < 0.05).
These are Type I errors,
giving an estimated family-wise error rate of
29.4%.

#### 3


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
error_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  fit <- aov(value ~ group, data = dat)
  test_tukey <- rstatix::tukey_hsd(fit)

  error_tukey[i] <- any(test_tukey$p.adj < 0.05)
}

mean(error_tukey)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.053
```


:::
:::


After Tukey's HSD adjustment, at least one pairwise comparison
provided statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean
difference in 53 of the 1,000 simulations
(adjusted p < 0.05).
Since all population means were zero, these are Type I errors,
and the estimated family-wise error rate is
5.3%.


### Part b


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
error_bh <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  test_bh <- pairwise.t.test(
    dat$value, dat$group,
    p.adjust.method = "BH"
  )

  error_bh[i] <- any(
    test_bh$p.value < 0.05,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}

mean(error_bh)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.047
```


:::
:::


After BH adjustment, at least one pairwise comparison provided
statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean difference
in 47 of the 1,000 simulations, giving an estimated
family-wise error rate of 4.7%.
This was much lower than the unadjusted rate of
29.4% and close to Tukey's
rate of 5.3%.

BH targets the false discovery rate (FDR), whereas Tukey's HSD
controls the family-wise error rate (FWER). 

## Question 2

### Part a


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Required sample size per group
pwr::pwr.anova.test(
  k = 5,
  f = 0.25,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Balanced one-way analysis of variance power calculation 

              k = 5
              n = 39.1534
              f = 0.25
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8

NOTE: n is number in each group
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Power curve
n <- 2:100

power <- sapply(n, function(x) {
  pwr::pwr.anova.test(
    k = 5, n = x, f = 0.25, sig.level = 0.05
  )$power
})

plot(n, power, type = "l",
     xlab = "Sample size per group",
     ylab = "Power",
     main = "ANOVA Power Curve")

abline(h = 0.80, col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = 40, col = "blue", lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HW2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The required sample size is roughly 40 participants per group and 200 in total.
The graph shows that 40 participants per group achieves slightly
more than 80% power.

Since every group in the original groups had more than 40
participants, the study is powered for the overall
ANOVA under the assumed moderate effect size. This calculation
assumes equal group sizes, so it does not provide the exact power
of the original unequal-sized design.


### Part b


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Non-centrality parameter and power
lambda <- 150 * 0.25^2
lambda
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9.375
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
critical <- qf(0.95, 4, 145)
pf(critical, 4, 145, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.6675964
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Alternative F distribution
curve(df(x, 4, 145, ncp = lambda), from = 0, to = 10,
      xlab = "F", ylab = "Density",
      main = "Alternative F Distribution: N = 150")
abline(v = critical, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HW2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


With 30 participants per group, the non-centrality parameter is
9.375 and the power is approximately 66.8%. Therefore, N = 150
is insufficient to achieve the desired 80% power.

### Part c


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Power for different sample sizes per group
n <- 40:500

power_c <- sapply(n, function(x) {
  PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test(
    n = x,
    groups = 5,
    delta = 0.25,
    within.var = 0.7152,
    sig.level = 0.05
  )$power
})

# Power with 40 participants per group
power_c[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.07866837
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Smallest sample size achieving at least 80% power
n_required <- min(n[power_c >= 0.80])
n_required
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 293
```


:::
:::


An overall ANOVA can detect differences among groups having different
means. However, detecting the smaller difference between
stages 1 and 2 is harder, especially after Tukey's adjustment
for multiple comparisons.

With 40 participants per group, the power is only about 7.9%.
Using the pooled variance of 0.7152, approximately 293 participants
per group are needed to achieve 80% power for this comparison.

### Part d


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(Superpower)

for (n in c(40, 80)) {

  design <- ANOVA_design(
    design = "5b",
    n = n,
    mu = c(2.92, 3.11, 3.36, 4.04, 4.35),
    sd = sqrt(0.80),
    plot = FALSE
  )

  result <- ANOVA_power(
    design,
    nsims = 1000,
    seed = 354,
    emm = TRUE,
    emm_p_adjust = "tukey",
    verbose = FALSE
  )

  print(paste("Sample size per group:", n))
  print(result$main_result)
  print(result$emm_results)
}
```

## Question 3

### Part a

Let $\mu_{2C}$, $\mu_{6C}$, $\mu_{16C}$, and $\mu_{16T}$ denote
the population mean SUVmax values for the 2-month control,
6-month control, 16-month control, and 16-month treatment groups,
respectively.

$$
H_0: \mu_{2C} = \mu_{6C} = \mu_{16C} = \mu_{16T}
$$

$$
H_a: \text{At least one population mean differs.}
$$

### Part b


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat3 <- data.frame(
  SUVmax = c(
    1.48969, 1.30168, 1.30620,
    4.36000, 4.28807, 3.64184,
    7.30182, 7.12416, 8.28764,
    4.69304, 2.51326, 2.38019
  ),
  group = factor(
    rep(c("2M Control", "6M Control",
          "16M Control", "16M Treatment"), each = 3),
    levels = c("2M Control", "6M Control",
               "16M Control", "16M Treatment")
  )
)

# Means and standard deviations
aggregate(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3, FUN = mean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
          group   SUVmax
1    2M Control 1.365857
2    6M Control 4.096637
3   16M Control 7.571207
4 16M Treatment 3.195497
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
aggregate(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3, FUN = sd)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
          group    SUVmax
1    2M Control 0.1072666
2    6M Control 0.3955041
3   16M Control 0.6267761
4 16M Treatment 1.2986162
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Display all observations
stripchart(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3,
           vertical = TRUE, method = "stack", pch = 19,
           xlab = "Group", ylab = "Heart SUVmax",
           main = "Heart SUVmax by Age and Treatment",
           cex.axis = 0.8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HW2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Among the control groups, mean heart SUVmax increased with age
(approximately 1.37, 4.10, and 7.57 for 2, 6, and 16 months,
respectively). The 16-month treatment group had a lower mean
(approximately 3.20) than the 16-month control group, placing it
between the two younger control groups.

### Part c


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
test3 <- oneway.test(SUVmax ~ group, data = dat3)
test3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)

data:  SUVmax and group
F = 98.464, num df = 3.0000, denom df = 3.5496, p-value = 0.0006851
```


:::
:::


SUVmax is quantitative. The sample standard deviations differ
substantially across groups, so I used Welch's ANOVA because it does
not assume equal population variances. The rats are not connected in certain ways so I assume independence. The observations per group are three, which is low, so the results should be interpreted cautiously.

Welch's ANOVA gives
$F = 98.46$,
with 3 and
3.55 degrees of freedom
(p = 6.85\times 10^{-4}).
Since p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The data provide
statistically discernible support that at least one population
mean heart SUVmax differs among the four groups.

### Part d


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
posthoc3 <- rstatix::games_howell_test(
  dat3, SUVmax ~ group
)

posthoc3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 8
  .y.    group1      group2     estimate conf.low conf.high   p.adj p.adj.signif
* <chr>  <chr>       <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>       
1 SUVmax 2M Control  6M Control    2.73      1.31     4.15  0.0119  *           
2 SUVmax 2M Control  16M Contr…    6.21      3.81     8.60  0.00720 **          
3 SUVmax 2M Control  16M Treat…    1.83     -3.30     6.96  0.308   ns          
4 SUVmax 6M Control  16M Contr…    3.47      1.56     5.39  0.00801 **          
5 SUVmax 6M Control  16M Treat…   -0.901    -5.47     3.67  0.698   ns          
6 SUVmax 16M Control 16M Treat…   -4.38     -8.51    -0.244 0.0431  *           
```


:::
:::


Games–Howell comparisons showed statistically discernible increases in mean heart SUVmax across the control groups: 2 versus 6 months (adjusted p = 0.0119), 2 versus 16 months (p = 0.0072), and 6 versus 16 months (p = 0.00801). The 16-month treatment group had a lower mean than the 16-month control group (estimated difference = −4.38, adjusted p = 0.0431), supporting a reduction associated with low-dose nicotine.

The treatment group did not differ significantly from the 2-month or 6-month control groups (adjusted p = 0.308 and 0.698, respectively), but these results do not establish equivalence to younger mice.

### Part e

The results support the hypothesis that SUVmax increases with age and is reduced by low-dose nicotine in older mice. All three control groups differed significantly, with higher mean SUVmax at older ages. Although the treatment group did not differ significantly from the younger controls, this does not establish that treatment restored SUVmax to younger levels.
